units.title: Unit 17 — People: character and behaviour
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 38–39 (PDF pages 42–43).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: People and relationships · character and behaviour
learningObjectives: Describe positive, negative and context-dependent personality traits with conventional adjective–noun and adverb–adjective pairings.
Use verb–noun expressions to describe keeping promises, emotional reactions, pranks and interpersonal behaviour.
Distinguish losing your temper from keeping it, and explain figurative phrases such as swallow your pride and bear a grudge.
Choose appropriate tone and register when describing people, including brutally honest, painfully shy and supremely confident.

items.pt: boa companhia; pessoa agradável de se ter por perto
items.example: Leila is good company on long journeys because she listens and tells interesting stories.
items.note: Describes someone whose presence is enjoyable, not a successful commercial company.

items.pt: uma tendência egoísta; um lado egoísta
items.example: Even kind people can have a selfish streak when they feel threatened.
items.note: A streak is a recurring aspect of someone’s character; the adjective selfish carries criticism.

items.example: Her outgoing personality makes it easy for her to meet new colleagues.
items.note: Outgoing describes someone sociable and comfortable meeting people, not someone who is leaving.

items.example: He has a good sense of humour and often makes everyone laugh.
items.note: Sense of humour is the conventional expression for appreciating or making jokes; British spelling is humour.

items.example: My niece has a vivid imagination and invents fascinating stories.
items.note: Vivid suggests lively, detailed mental images; the usual pairing is vivid imagination.

items.pt: perder a paciência; perder a calma
items.example: Try not to lose your temper when a customer complains.
items.note: Means suddenly become angry; contrast with keep your temper and control your temper.

items.example: The new engineer is highly intelligent and learns unfamiliar systems quickly.
items.note: Highly is an established intensifier with intelligent; it is not interchangeable with every adjective.

items.pt: uma mente extremamente aguçada; raciocínio afiado
items.example: At eighty-five, my aunt still has a razor-sharp mind.
items.note: A figurative way to describe very quick, accurate thinking; razor-sharp is a compound adjective.

items.pt: estabelecer padrões elevados para si mesmo; ser muito exigente consigo
items.example: You can set high standards for yourself without expecting perfection every day.
items.note: The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: for myself, herself, themselves and so on.

items.pt: extremamente leal; leal de forma inabalável
items.example: Despite the disagreement, she remained fiercely loyal to her oldest friends.
items.note: Fiercely intensifies loyal and suggests powerful commitment, not physical aggression.

items.pt: colocar os outros em primeiro lugar; priorizar outras pessoas
items.example: He tends to put others first when decisions affect the whole team.
items.note: Put someone first means give their needs priority, often over your own.

items.example: I was painfully shy at school but grew more confident with practice.
items.note: Painfully intensifies shy; it does not refer to actual physical pain.

items.example: His brief replies gave the impression of impatience.
items.note: Follow of with a noun or -ing form; give the impression that introduces a clause.

items.pt: extremamente confiante; muito seguro de si
items.example: The pianist seemed supremely confident just before the concert.
items.note: Supremely is a strong intensifier, often suggesting an exceptional degree of confidence.

items.example: I have a tendency to speak too quickly when I am nervous.
items.note: The pattern is have a tendency to + infinitive; a tendency to make snap decisions is an example.

items.pt: tomar uma decisão precipitada; decidir de forma impulsiva
items.example: Do not make a snap decision about the job offer without checking the conditions.
items.note: Snap describes a decision made very quickly, perhaps without enough thought; use make, not do.

items.example: She has a strong sense of responsibility towards the people she supervises.
items.note: Sense of responsibility means feeling personally accountable for obligations or other people.

items.pt: cumprir sua palavra; manter o prometido
items.example: I trust him because he always keeps his word.
items.note: Keep your word means fulfil a promise; the possessive changes with the speaker.

items.example: Can you keep a secret until the announcement is made?
items.note: Keep a secret means not reveal confidential information; keeping secrets can describe an ability or a habit.

items.example: She chose not to bear a grudge after their argument.
items.note: Bear a grudge often takes against someone; it describes continuing resentment about a past offence.

items.pt: manter a calma; controlar o temperamento
items.example: Despite the criticism, she managed to keep her temper.
items.note: Means avoid becoming angry; it contrasts directly with lose your temper.

items.word: make a fool out of someone
items.pt: fazer alguém de bobo; ridicularizar alguém
items.example: The prank was meant to make a fool out of him in front of his friends.
items.note: Means make another person look silly. Make a fool of someone is also common.

items.pt: brutalmente sincero; franco a ponto de magoar
items.example: I asked for an opinion, and she was brutally honest about the design.
items.note: Brutally adds the idea that the honesty is direct enough to upset or hurt someone.

items.pt: magoar os sentimentos de alguém; ferir alguém emocionalmente
items.example: I did not want to hurt someone's feelings by laughing at the mistake.
items.note: Hurt feelings refers to emotional pain; the possessive changes according to the person affected.

items.pt: pregar uma peça em alguém; brincar com alguém
items.example: They decided to play a joke on their coach on his birthday.
items.note: Play a joke on someone is idiomatic for a prank; the unit warns against make a joke/trick in this sense.

items.pt: pregar uma peça em alguém; fazer uma pegadinha com alguém
items.example: The children played a trick on their older brother by changing his ringtone.
items.note: For a practical joke use play a trick on someone, not make a trick.

items.pt: saber levar uma brincadeira na esportiva
items.example: Our manager can take a joke and laughs at harmless teasing.
items.note: Describes being able to accept humour directed at oneself without becoming upset.

items.pt: engolir o orgulho; deixar o orgulho de lado
items.example: I had to swallow my pride and admit that my colleague was right.
items.note: Figurative expression for doing something despite feeling embarrassed or too proud.

items.pt: fazer birra; ter um ataque de raiva
items.example: The toddler threw a tantrum when it was time to leave the playground.
items.note: A tantrum is a sudden uncontrolled angry outburst, especially associated with young children.

items.example: She rarely loses her patience even when the instructions are confusing.
items.note: Lose your patience means stop tolerating a situation calmly; closely related to lose your temper.

items.pt: aceitar e assimilar uma situação difícil; aprender a lidar com
items.example: It took months to come to terms with the sudden change in his life.
items.note: A fixed expression meaning accept an unpleasant reality psychologically; with is essential.

items.pt: revelar seu verdadeiro caráter; mostrar quem realmente é
items.example: How she treated her colleagues under pressure revealed her true character.
items.note: Reveal means show a previously less visible side of someone; contrast with hide your true character.

items.example: He tried to hide his true character during the first weeks of the project.
items.note: The opposite of reveal your true character; conceal is a more formal alternative to hide.

items.example: I give you my word that I will finish the report by Friday.
items.note: A conventional way of making a firm promise; keep your word means honour that promise.

items.example: He has a bad temper, so small delays can make him angry.
items.note: Bad temper describes a tendency to become angry easily; foul temper is a stronger alternative.

items.pt: controlar o temperamento; conter a raiva
items.example: She learned to control her temper during stressful discussions.
items.note: Control your temper means regulate anger; related to keep your temper.

items.pt: senso de dever; sentido de obrigação
items.example: A strong sense of duty kept her at work until the problem was resolved.
items.note: Sense of duty means feeling morally or professionally obliged to act.

items.pt: senso de honra; sentimento de honra
items.example: He refused the offer because of his sense of honour.
items.note: British spelling honour; the expression refers to moral integrity and personal principles.

items.example: The teacher has a sense of fun that makes the lessons enjoyable.
items.note: Describes a playful attitude, not the same as sense of humour, though they are related.

items.pt: os ânimos ficam exaltados; a paciência se esgota
items.example: Tempers get frayed when everyone is tired and the meeting runs late.
items.note: Often used in the past form tempers got frayed; the figurative image suggests growing irritation.

units.title: Unit 18 — People: physical appearance
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 40–41 (PDF pages 44–45).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: People and relationships · physical appearance
learningObjectives: Describe faces, noses, hair, body shape and general grooming with natural adjective–noun collocations.
Distinguish similar descriptive adjectives, especially slim/slender, coarse/sleek and fair/dark.
Use conventional phrases for changes in hair, resemblance and memorable appearance.
Recognise connotations and restrictions, including the potentially negative dumpy and the use of ginger or auburn for hair.

items.example: My brother has a round face and a cheerful smile.
items.note: Round describes the overall shape of the face; contrast with a pointed or oval face.

items.pt: bigode caído; bigode com pontas caídas
items.example: The actor wore a droopy moustache for the historical drama.
items.note: Droopy means hanging down; British English uses moustache.

items.pt: rosto pontudo; rosto de traços afilados
items.example: Her pointed face makes her look rather different from her round-faced sister.
items.note: Pointed describes a face that becomes narrow towards the chin; contrast with round face.

items.example: She has a straight nose like her father.
items.note: Straight describes the shape of the nose; the unit contrasts it with an upturned nose.

items.example: He has an oval face and short curly hair.
items.note: Oval refers to an egg-like face outline; an oval face is a common descriptive phrase.

items.example: The child has an upturned nose and a broad smile.
items.note: Upturned means the tip points slightly upwards; contrast with a straight nose.

items.example: She has a lovely complexion and rarely wears make-up.
items.note: Complexion refers to the natural appearance and condition of facial skin, not facial shape.

items.example: His bushy eyebrows give his face a distinctive look.
items.note: Bushy means thick and abundant; it naturally collocates with eyebrows.

items.example: The toddler has chubby cheeks and a bright smile.
items.note: Chubby usually suggests a rounded shape in a friendly or affectionate way, especially for children.

items.pt: cabelo liso e brilhante; cabelo sedoso
items.example: She brushed her sleek hair before leaving the house.
items.note: Sleek describes smooth, neat, shiny hair; contrast with coarse hair.

items.example: He had shoulder-length hair when he was at university.
items.note: Shoulder-length is a hyphenated adjective placed before hair; it describes the hair’s length.

items.example: He uses conditioner because his hair is naturally coarse.
items.note: Coarse describes a rough, thick texture; unlike sleek, it does not mean smooth.

items.example: Even at seventy, she still has thick hair.
items.note: Thick hair means plenty of hair or dense strands; it does not necessarily mean coarse hair.

items.example: Both sisters have dark hair, although one has blue eyes.
items.note: Dark describes hair colour; contrast with fair hair, which refers to a lighter shade.

items.pt: cabelo preto intenso; cabelo bem preto
items.example: The singer had jet-black hair that stood out against her pale jacket.
items.note: Jet-black means intensely black; it is more emphatic than simply dark.

items.pt: ficar grisalho; começar a ter cabelos brancos
items.example: He began to go grey in his late thirties.
items.note: Go grey is the natural change-of-state combination for hair; British spelling is grey.

items.example: She had fair hair as a child, but it became darker with age.
items.note: Fair here means light-coloured, particularly blond or light brown hair; contrast with dark hair.

items.example: He has ginger hair and freckles across his nose.
items.note: Ginger describes a red-orange hair colour; for people it is used specifically of hair, and tone can vary by context.

items.example: Her auburn hair looks reddish in the afternoon light.
items.note: Auburn is a reddish-brown hair colour; the textbook flags it as a hair-specific adjective.

items.example: She has blonde hair and usually wears it tied back.
items.note: Blonde is a conventional hair-colour adjective; it is not normally used of unrelated objects.

items.example: He arrived with dishevelled hair after running through the rain.
items.note: Dishevelled suggests noticeable untidiness; it can also describe a person’s overall appearance.

items.pt: impecavelmente arrumado; muito bem cuidado na aparência
items.example: The presenter was immaculately groomed for the interview.
items.note: Immaculately is an adverb meaning perfectly or extremely neatly; groomed concerns personal appearance.

items.example: She has a slim figure and enjoys swimming regularly.
items.note: Slim suggests being attractively thin; avoid assuming it describes fitness or health.

items.example: The dress had a narrow belt around her slender waist.
items.note: Slender is a rather formal or literary adjective for attractively slim proportions.

items.example: She chose trousers designed for people with broad hips.
items.note: Broad is a common descriptive partner for hips and shoulders; it does not imply a judgement about appearance.

items.pt: bem constituído fisicamente; de porte forte
items.example: The well-built cyclist carried the heavy bicycle upstairs easily.
items.note: Well-built typically describes a strong, solid physique, and it can be used of people without judging attractiveness.

items.example: The jacket was tight because he has broad shoulders.
items.note: Broad shoulders is the conventional phrase for a wide upper-body build.

items.example: His grandfather started to go bald when he was young.
items.note: Go bald describes a change in appearance; get bald is not the normal collocation.

items.example: She has a youthful appearance despite being in her sixties.
items.note: Youthful describes looking younger than might be expected, not necessarily being young.

items.example: The novel describes a dumpy woman waiting outside the station.
items.note: Dumpy refers to a short, fairly round build and may sound unkind or judgemental; use cautiously.

items.pt: um senhor corpulento; um homem de meia-idade ou idoso e corpulento
items.example: A portly gentleman in a dark coat greeted the guests.
items.note: Portly is a somewhat formal description of a rounded or heavy build, traditionally used for older men.

items.pt: um jovem alto e desengonçado; rapaz alto e magro
items.example: A lanky youth stood at the back of the queue.
items.note: Lanky suggests being tall, thin and sometimes awkward in movement.

items.pt: uma semelhança impressionante; uma semelhança muito marcante
items.example: There is a striking resemblance between the two brothers.
items.note: Striking means immediately noticeable; bear a striking resemblance to is a common fuller expression.

items.pt: ter uma semelhança impressionante com; ser muito parecido com
items.example: She bears a striking resemblance to her grandmother in old photographs.
items.note: The pattern is bear a striking resemblance to someone; resemblance, not resemblance with, takes to here.

items.pt: uma aparência marcante; um visual impressionante
items.example: The dancer had a striking appearance that everyone remembered.
items.note: Striking describes a memorable and often attractive appearance; it is not automatically negative.

items.example: The tailor adjusted the jacket to fit her slim waist.
items.note: Slim and slender can both describe a waist; slender is often more formal.
